name: Post-validation Peer-review Dialogue Plan
description: Adaptive post-validation dialogue covering seven peer-review reasoning categories across two reviews.
title: Post-validation Dialogue
completionMessage: Thank you. The dialogue is complete.

categories.label: Understanding the reviewed work
categories.evidenceGoal: The student explains what they understood the reviewed exposé to be trying to do.

categories.label: Criteria used for judgment
categories.evidenceGoal: The student explains the standard or criterion used to judge quality.

categories.label: Evidence grounding
categories.evidenceGoal: The student connects their feedback to evidence or features in the reviewed exposé.

categories.label: Judgment justification and challenge
categories.evidenceGoal: The student explains and defends why a review judgment follows.

categories.label: Constructive implications
categories.evidenceGoal: The student explains what would improve if the author followed the feedback.

categories.label: Assumptions, uncertainty, and limits
categories.evidenceGoal: The student identifies assumptions, uncertainty, or limits in their own review.

categories.label: Review strategy and reflection
categories.sourceCategory: Socratic questions about the question and reflection
categories.evidenceGoal: The student explains how they decided what to focus on and how they approached the review.

questions.text: Thinking about the first review you submitted, what did you understand as the main aim or main problem of the exposé?
questions.help: Summarize what you understood the exposé to be trying to do. There is no required wording.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student explains their understanding of the reviewed work.
questions.completeWhen: The answer names the main aim, problem, claim, or focus of the exposé and explains it in the student's own words.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask the student to clarify the main claim, goal, or problem they understood.

questions.text: Thinking about the second review you submitted, what criteria did you use to judge whether something was strong, weak, clear, unclear, supported, or unsupported?
questions.help: Explain the standards or qualities you used when making your judgments.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student explains the criterion or quality standard behind the judgment.
questions.completeWhen: The answer names at least one standard or criterion used to judge quality.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask what standard the student compared the work against.

questions.text: Thinking about the first review you submitted, what evidence from the exposé supported one of your judgments?
questions.anchoredText: In your first review, you wrote: “{{anchor}}” What in the exposé led you to write this feedback?
questions.help: You can mention a specific claim, section, example, missing detail, or piece of evidence in the exposé.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student connects their feedback to evidence or features in the reviewed exposé.
questions.completeWhen: The answer points to a claim, section, missing evidence, unclear wording, weak structure, or unsupported conclusion.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask for the specific claim, section, evidence, wording, or missing element that led to the feedback.

questions.text: Thinking about the second review you submitted, why was one of your main points important enough to include?
questions.anchoredText: In your second review, you wrote: “{{anchor}}” Why was this point important enough to include?
questions.help: Explain why the quoted point mattered for the quality or usefulness of the exposé.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student explains and defends the importance of a review judgment.
questions.completeWhen: The answer explains why the point matters for the quality, clarity, argument, evidence, or usefulness of the exposé.
questions.followUpDirection: If shallow, ask how the student would defend the point if the author disagreed.

questions.text: Thinking about the first review you submitted, choose one suggestion you made. What would improve in the exposé if the author followed it?
questions.help: First identify one suggestion from your review, then explain the change you expected it to produce.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student explains the intended improvement behind the feedback.
questions.completeWhen: The answer explains a concrete expected improvement in evidence, structure, argument, method, clarity, or reader understanding.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask what concrete change would happen in the argument, evidence, structure, clarity, or reader understanding.

questions.text: Thinking about the second review you submitted, where were you least sure about your own review, and why?
questions.help: You can mention missing information, an assumption, or another possible interpretation.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student identifies uncertainty, assumptions, or limits in their own judgment.
questions.completeWhen: The answer names an uncertainty, assumption, missing information, alternative interpretation, or limitation in the student's own review.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask what assumption, missing information, or alternative interpretation made the student uncertain.

questions.text: Thinking about the first review you submitted, how did you decide what to focus on first?
questions.help: Describe how you chose which issues to prioritize while reviewing.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student explains their review strategy and prioritization.
questions.completeWhen: The answer explains how the student selected priorities for the review.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask how the student chose between several possible issues.

questions.text: When you compare the two reviews you submitted, did you use the same standards, or did your approach change?
questions.help: Compare the standards or reviewing approach you used across both reviews.
questions.evidenceGoal: The student compares standards, strategy, or reasoning across both peer reviews.
questions.completeWhen: The answer explains whether the student's standards, focus, uncertainty, or review strategy stayed the same or changed.
questions.followUpDirection: If vague, ask what changed and why, or what stayed the same across both reviews.
